Let’s dive into Chapter 1: Why Innovation Often Feels Like a Gamble.
Have you ever noticed how, in business, innovation can feel a lot like rolling the dice?
Companies pour tons of energy—and money—into launching new products or services, all hoping to catch your eye and outpace their rivals.
But even with meticulous planning and mountains of research, so many of these big ideas just... fall flat.
It’s no wonder people start to think that winning at innovation is all about luck, rather than something you can actually predict or control.
But here’s the thing most people miss: at the core of all this uncertainty is a fundamental misconception about what really drives customer decisions.
Most organizations focus on stacking up features, tacking on the latest technology, or trying to one-up the competition. They study market reports, run surveys, and pile up data—hoping that, if they just analyze enough, the path to success will reveal itself.
Yet, all this effort often skips something essential: customers aren’t just buying products or services—they’re actually “hiring” them to solve a problem or fill a specific need in their lives.
Picture this: you’re standing in front of a shelf full of drinks. What’ll you grab? It’s rarely just about taste, or price, right?
Maybe you need something quick to sip on the way to work. Maybe you want that refreshment after a tough workout. Or maybe, after a long day, you’re just looking to treat yourself.
Each of those moments is a different “job” you’re trying to get done. And the drink that matches your need—that’s the one you’ll pick.
This way of looking at things shifts the spotlight away from the product itself, and onto the context where it’s used.
So, instead of brainstorming endless new features, innovation should really start by understanding the progress your customer is trying to make.
When companies miss this point, they end up offering solutions that look great on paper—but don’t actually matter in real life.
That’s why innovation so often feels random. When you don’t truly understand why customers choose one option over another, even the smartest strategies can turn into little more than a guessing game.
If you want to move past luck, you’ve got to dig deep and uncover the real motivations that make people “hire” one solution instead of another.
This means looking past old-school categories like age groups or price points. Instead of asking, “What do millennials want?” or “How can we beat the competition on cost?”, try asking, “What’s the job this person needs to get done—and how can we help them do it better?”
By flipping the challenge like this, you’ll start to see patterns that were hidden before—and you’ll design products and services that truly connect with people.
So, here’s the key takeaway: the road to reliable, predictable innovation begins by realizing that customer choices aren’t random at all.
They’re shaped by the unique situations people face, and the progress they’re aiming for.
And when you understand those dynamics, you can finally build offerings that succeed—not by chance, but by design.
